newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia markets rally as Clinton, Republicans win.
newsitem.headline: Asia markets rally as Clinton, Republicans win.

text.p: Asian markets moved higher on Wednesday after U.S. President Bill Clinton swept to victory and Republicans appeared to retain control of Congress, something traders view as positive for financial markets.
Before voting ended in California, U.S. television polls predicted Clinton the winner. At 0410 GMT he had captured 367 electoral votes, more than the 270 required.

Exit polls also indicated the Republican party would remain in control of Congress, a situation traders view as favourable for financial markets since it suggests there will not be any jolts to the U.S. economy from new fiscal policies.
Most Asian markets took their cue from U.S. markets, where similar sentiments on Tuesday prompted powerful rallies in U.S. government bonds and on Wall Street.
"It's the Dow Jones that pushed us up today, the election results were pretty much expected," said Bobby Ho, chief dealer at G.K. Goh Securities in Hong Kong.
Percy Au-Young, research director at DBS Securities, noted that a correction after the U.S. election was forecast and that the Hang Seng could fall to 12,200 again.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 91.54 points, or 0.73 percent, to 12,594.24.
Hedge funds and foreign buying led the rally in U.S. government bonds, with the key 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond up one point to yield 6.59 percent, down from 6.66 percent on Monday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 39.50 points in New York overnight to close at 6,081.18.

On Wednesday, U.S. Treasuries and the dollar moved higher in Tokyo, with the long bond yielding 6.57 percent, while the dollar recovered to 114.00 yen by midday in Tokyo after falling below that level in early trade.
It closed at 114.20/25 yen in New York on Tuesday.
In Tokyo, shares opened slightly higher and climbed further in the early afternoon, with the Nikkei 225 share average up 313.44 points, or 1.52 percent, at 20,905.77.
"The (Japanese) domestic political sphere is still unclear and that is going to be a heavier burden than the U.S. presidential election," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is to be formally re-elected prime minister in a special session of parliament on Thursday. He must form a minority government after failing to put together a new coalition.
Jakarta shares opened firmer following active buying of Telkom in New York overnight. The Jakarta Composite Index was up 2.54 points, or 0.44 percent, to 586.41.

Thai stocks moved higher in early trade amid optimism that a meeting on Wednesday among the Bank of Thailand, banks and finance companies will be positive for the property sector. The SET index gained 13.24 points, or 1.44 percent, to 932.25.
Taiwan share prices rallied on buying of financial sector stocks, with the weighted index up 49.51 points, or 0.75 percent, at 6,653.65.
Philippine shares inched higher after opening mixed, with the main index up 11.25 points, or 0.38 percent, at 2998.43.
Malaysian blue chips were lower with the Composite Index down 1.38 points, or 0.12 percent, at 1175.43.

In Singapore, shares opened flat, but later fell to be off 1.43 points, or 0.07 percent, to 2068.80. Late Tuesday, Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said third-quarter growth was 3.2 percent against the second-quarter's 7.5 percent.
Korean shares posted gains on bargain hunting after tumbling for two consecutive days. The KSE index was up 12.00 points, or 1.64 percent, at 745.65.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index was off 1.0 points, or 0.04 percent, at 2,360.6, while New Zealand shares were up 13.75 points, or 0.59 percent, at 2,325.21.
